title: Publishing BuildLog when CLI and GitHub Desktop used different authentication
goal: Publish the approved BuildLog baseline commits to the intended existing GitHub repository without changing the remote, committing local artifacts, or creating another repository.
context: The BuildLog commits were complete locally on master, and GitHub Desktop already had an authenticated user session. The command-line GitHub client did not share that authenticated state.
problem: A command-line push to the HTTPS origin failed because Git could not read a GitHub username from the current environment. GitHub CLI also reported that no GitHub host was authenticated, even though GitHub Desktop was signed in.
actions: Reviewed git status, the configured branch, and the intended repository URL before attempting to publish.
Kept the existing origin URL unchanged.
Ran the complete tests and diff checks before each commit.
Staged only source, documentation, prompts, configuration, examples, and tests.
Left .venv, buildlog.db, caches, generated runs, and local artifacts outside the commits.
Attempted the HTTPS push from the command line and captured the authentication failure.
Checked GitHub CLI authentication and confirmed that it was not logged in.
Used the already authenticated GitHub Desktop session for the manual push.
Verified the remote master hash with git ls-remote after the Desktop push.

decisions.decision: Use the authenticated GitHub Desktop session instead of changing repository configuration.
decisions.reason: The repository and commits were correct; the blocker was the command-line authentication context.
alternatives_considered: Store a personal access token in the project.

decisions.decision: Verify the remote commit after the manual push.
decisions.reason: A clean local status alone does not prove that the expected commit reached GitHub.
alternatives_considered: Assume the Desktop success indicator was sufficient.

trade_offs: The final publish step required a manual action in GitHub Desktop.
GitHub CLI remained unauthenticated after the repository was published.
Desktop and command-line authentication can behave differently even in the same local repository.
result: Both BuildLog baseline commits reached the existing origin on master. The final remote hash matched d00d8ebb3f9c0bba3e34e65a122087bdf52c5b53, and the local branch reported no divergence from origin/master.
lessons: Repository state and authentication state are separate failure domains.
A GUI client login does not imply that Git or GitHub CLI can reuse the same credentials.
A manual publishing step can be acceptable when it is explicit, minimal, and followed by a remote hash check.
Generated model artifacts should stay out of a source commit even when they are central to the experiment.
evidence: The command-line push failed with: could not read Username for 'https://github.com': Device not configured.
GitHub CLI reported that it was not logged into any GitHub hosts.
The architecture baseline commit is ff99f826bb29924e1f1b02cbd420e27038fa2181.
The output-quality baseline commit is d00d8ebb3f9c0bba3e34e65a122087bdf52c5b53.
A remote refs/heads/master lookup returned d00d8ebb3f9c0bba3e34e65a122087bdf52c5b53.
The final local status was master...origin/master with no tracked changes.
audience: Software engineers working across local Git tools and authenticated desktop clients
